JOINT AUTHORSHIP AND COPYRIGHT CO-OWNERSHIP — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan T. Reyes · A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015.

PURPOSE OF THIS JOINT AUTHORSHIP AND COPYRIGHT CO-OWNERSHIP INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes the federal rules on joint authorship and co-ownership of copyright -- the statutory definition of a "joint work" in 17 U.S.C. § 101, the rule in 17 U.S.C. § 201(a) that the authors of a joint work are co-owners of its copyright, the Ninth Circuit's test for who counts as an "author" of a joint work under Aalmuhammed v. Lee, the default rules governing what a co-owner of a copyright may do without the other co-owners' consent (independent use and nonexclusive licensing, subject to a duty to account for profits) under Oddo v. Ries and Sybersound Records, Inc. v. UAV Corp., the limits on a single co-owner's power to grant an exclusive license or transfer more than its own interest, the copyright term for joint works under 17 U.S.C. § 302(b), and the written-instrument requirement for transfers of copyright ownership under 17 U.S.C. § 204(a). It is prepared by Jordan T. Reyes concerning the following work: A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015., to which the following persons contributed: Maria Chen (directed and edited the film); Devon Okafor (wrote the narration script); Sam Patel (composed the original score). This Information Sheet describes what the statute and the cited federal appellate decisions say; it does not itself determine whether the work described above is a joint work, whether any particular contributor is one of its authors or co-owners, or what any contributor's rights or obligations are in any specific dispute, and it is not a substitute for that case-specific legal determination.

THE STATUTORY DEFINITION OF A "JOINT WORK"
The Copyright Act defines a "joint work" as a work prepared by two or more authors with the intention that their contributions be merged into inseparable or interdependent parts of a unitary whole. On the statute's face, the definition turns on three things: more than one author, contributions that are merged into a single unitary work (whether the parts are inseparable, like a jointly written novel, or merely interdependent, like the words and music of a song), and an intention -- held at the time the contributions are made -- that they be so merged. The definition uses the word "authors," and a companion clause in this Information Sheet describes how the Ninth Circuit has read that word to require more than a valuable or even copyrightable contribution.

INITIAL OWNERSHIP: THE AUTHORS OF A JOINT WORK ARE CO-OWNERS OF THE COPYRIGHT
Copyright vests initially in the author or authors of a work, and the Copyright Act provides in a single sentence that the authors of a joint work are co-owners of the copyright in the work. Co-ownership under this provision arises automatically from joint authorship, without any agreement or registration -- it is a consequence of the work's status as a joint work. The provision does not itself say what each co-owner may do with the copyright or how co-owners' interests are divided; the courts have supplied those default rules, which are described in companion clauses of this Information Sheet, and the statute's legislative history, as quoted by the Ninth Circuit, describes co-owners as being treated generally as tenants in common.

THE NINTH CIRCUIT'S THREE ELEMENTS OF A JOINT WORK AND THE INDEPENDENTLY COPYRIGHTABLE CONTRIBUTION REQUIREMENT
In Aalmuhammed v. Lee, the Ninth Circuit read the statutory definition as establishing three elements of a joint work: a copyrightable work, two or more "authors," and an intention by those authors that their contributions be merged into inseparable or interdependent parts of a unitary whole. The court also restated the rule in the Ninth Circuit that a joint work requires each author to make an independently copyrightable contribution to the disputed work. Applying that rule to the case before it -- a claim by a consultant on the motion picture Malcolm X that he was a co-author of the film -- the court observed that some kinds of help, such as speaking Arabic to persons in charge of a mosque or coaching actors, do not result in a copyrightable contribution unless turned into an expression in a form subject to copyright, while rewritten dialogue and written scenes that appeared in the film would, if the claimant's evidence were accepted, be independently copyrightable.

AUTHORSHIP IS REQUIRED, AND IT IS NOT THE SAME THING AS MAKING A VALUABLE, COPYRIGHTABLE CONTRIBUTION
The central holding of Aalmuhammed v. Lee is that the statutory definition of a joint work requires "authors," and that being an author is not the same thing as making a valuable and copyrightable contribution to the work. The court accepted, for purposes of summary judgment, that the claimant had contributed substantially to the film and had presented a genuine issue of fact on whether his contributions were copyrightable, and that everyone involved intended his contributions to be merged into the film as a unitary whole -- and nonetheless held that he had not shown he was one of the film's authors. The court distinguished between a contributor being deemed the author of a particular expression for the limited purpose of deciding whether that expression is independently copyrightable, and the different and larger question of whether the contributor is an author of the joint work within the meaning of the statute.

THE AALMUHAMMED FACTORS: CONTROL, OBJECTIVE MANIFESTATIONS OF SHARED INTENT, AND AUDIENCE APPEAL
Drawing on the Supreme Court's nineteenth-century definition of an author as the person to whom a work owes its origin and who superintended the whole work, the Ninth Circuit in Aalmuhammed v. Lee identified several factors as among the criteria for joint authorship in the absence of a contract. First, an author superintends the work by exercising control -- the person who actually forms the work, the inventive or master mind who creates or gives effect to the idea. Second, putative co-authors make objective manifestations of a shared intent to be co-authors, such as billing a work as the product of both (the court's example is "Gilbert and Sullivan"); the court explained that it looks to objective manifestations rather than subjective intent because a subjective test could become an instrument of fraud if one co-author hid an intention to take sole credit. Third, the audience appeal of the work turns on both contributions, so that the share of each in its success cannot be appraised. The court stated that control will in many cases be the most important factor.

A CONTRACT IS THE BEST OBJECTIVE MANIFESTATION OF INTENT; ABSENCE OF CONTROL IS STRONG EVIDENCE AGAINST CO-AUTHORSHIP
The Ninth Circuit in Aalmuhammed v. Lee stated that the best objective manifestation of a shared intent to be co-authors is a contract saying that the parties intend to be, or not to be, co-authors, and that in the absence of a contract the inquiry must focus on the facts. The court cautioned that its factors cannot be reduced to a rigid formula, because creative relationships vary too much and can change over time as a work proceeds. Applying the factors, the court found that the claimant never had superintendence of the film -- the studio and the director controlled it -- and that although the claimant could make extremely helpful recommendations, the director was not bound to accept any of them. The court described the claimant's lack of control over the work as strong evidence of the absence of co-authorship, and noted that no one had made any objective manifestation, before litigation, that the claimant was intended to be a co-author and co-owner.

DEFAULT RULE: A CO-OWNER CANNOT INFRINGE THE CO-OWNED COPYRIGHT AND MAY INDEPENDENTLY USE OR LICENSE IT
Under the Ninth Circuit's decision in Oddo v. Ries, a co-owner of a copyright cannot be liable to another co-owner for infringement of that copyright; rather, each co-owner has an independent right to use the copyright or to license others to use it. The court applied this rule to two partners whose partnership owned the copyrights in a manuscript and a book, holding that one partner's publication of the book could not infringe the partnership's copyrights that he co-owned, so that his use of those copyrights could not form the basis for any award under the Copyright Act. The same default rule appears in the legislative history of the 1976 Copyright Act, which -- as quoted by the Ninth Circuit in Sybersound Records, Inc. v. UAV Corp. -- describes co-owners of a copyright as treated generally as tenants in common, each with an independent right to use or license the use of the work, subject to a duty of accounting to the other co-owners for any profits.

THE DUTY TO ACCOUNT FOR PROFITS ARISES FROM STATE LAW, NOT FROM THE COPYRIGHT ACT
The Ninth Circuit in Oddo v. Ries stated that a co-owner of a copyright must account to the other co-owners for any profits the co-owner earns from licensing or use of the copyright, but that this duty to account does not derive from the copyright law's prohibition of infringement. Instead, the court said, it comes from equitable doctrines relating to unjust enrichment and general principles of law governing the rights of co-owners. The court drew a jurisdictional consequence from this: a suit to bring the co-owner of a copyright to account does not fall within the federal district courts' jurisdiction over actions arising under the copyright law, although in the case before it the court noted that the district court could consider exercising pendent jurisdiction over the accounting claim alongside a related infringement claim.

CO-OWNERSHIP RULES APPLY BEYOND JOINT AUTHORS, INCLUDING TO PARTNERS UNDER CALIFORNIA PARTNERSHIP LAW
Joint authorship is one way copyright co-ownership arises, but not the only way. In Oddo v. Ries, the two co-owners were not joint authors -- one partner wrote the manuscript and the other supplied capital and business supervision -- and the copyrights were owned by their partnership, so that each partner was a co-owner of the partnership's assets under the California Corporations Code provision then in force. The Ninth Circuit saw no reason to exclude partners from the general rules governing copyright co-ownership and noted that those rules had already been applied to co-owners who were not joint authors. The court added that a co-owner who misuses partnership copyrights may be liable to the other partner under California partnership law, but that a violation of state partnership law does not transform the co-owner's use of the copyrights into infringement under federal law.

A SINGLE CO-OWNER CAN GRANT ONLY A NONEXCLUSIVE LICENSE AND CANNOT TRANSFER MORE THAN ITS OWN INTEREST
In Sybersound Records, Inc. v. UAV Corp., the Ninth Circuit held that a co-owner of a copyright, acting alone, cannot grant an exclusive license: unless all the other co-owners join in granting the exclusive right, a single co-owner can grant only a nonexclusive license, because one co-owner may not limit the other co-owners' independent rights to exploit the copyright. The court applied this rule to a karaoke record producer that had taken an assignment of one co-owner's karaoke-use interest in nine songs, each of which had several other co-owners who had not joined the assignment. Because the assignment could convey only a nonexclusive license, the assignee was neither an exclusive licensee nor a co-owner and therefore lacked standing to sue for infringement. Separately, the Copyright Act provides that a transfer of copyright ownership, other than by operation of law, is not valid unless an instrument of conveyance, or a note or memorandum of the transfer, is in writing and signed by the owner of the rights conveyed or that owner's duly authorized agent -- a formality that applies to any co-owner's transfer of its own interest as well.

CONTRIBUTIONS MADE AS WORKS MADE FOR HIRE: THE EMPLOYER IS THE AUTHOR
The joint-authorship analysis described in this Information Sheet operates against the separate statutory rule for works made for hire. Under 17 U.S.C. § 201(b), in the case of a work made for hire the employer or other person for whom the work was prepared is considered the author, and, unless the parties have expressly agreed otherwise in a written instrument signed by them, owns all of the rights comprised in the copyright. The Ninth Circuit's opinion in Aalmuhammed v. Lee illustrates the interaction: the studio had required the director to sign a work-for-hire agreement, so that even the director would not be a co-author and co-owner with the studio, and the court found it illogical to conclude that the studio, while not permitting the director to own the copyright, intended to share ownership with individuals who worked under the director's control.

COPYRIGHT TERM FOR A JOINT WORK: LIFE OF THE LAST SURVIVING AUTHOR PLUS 70 YEARS
For a joint work prepared by two or more authors who did not work for hire, the copyright endures for a term consisting of the life of the last surviving author and 70 years after that author's death. This differs from the single-author term (the author's life plus 70 years) and from the fixed term for works made for hire, and it means that a finding of joint authorship can lengthen the copyright term of a work by keying its expiration to the longest-lived co-author.

citations.quote: We hold that because Sybersound is neither an exclusive licensee nor a co-owner in the nine copyrights, it lacks standing to bring the copyright infringement claims alleged in the FAC, and, thus, its copyright infringement claims fail.

citations.quote: A transfer of copyright ownership, other than by operation of law, is not valid unless an instrument of conveyance, or a note or memorandum of the transfer, is in writing and signed by the owner of the rights conveyed or such owner's duly authorized agent.

expectedJSON.body: The joint-authorship analysis described in this Information Sheet operates against the separate statutory rule for works made for hire. Under 17 U.S.C. § 201(b), in the case of a work made for hire the employer or other person for whom the work was prepared is considered the author, and, unless the parties have expressly agreed otherwise in a written instrument signed by them, owns all of the rights comprised in the copyright. The Ninth Circuit's opinion in Aalmuhammed v. Lee illustrates the interaction: the studio had required the director to sign a work-for-hire agreement, so that even the director would not be a co-author and co-owner with the studio, and the court found it illogical to conclude that the studio, while not permitting the director to own the copyright, intended to share ownership with individuals who worked under the director's control.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, Copyright Act, ownership of copyright -- works made for hire
citations.quote: In the case of a work made for hire, the employer or other person for whom the work was prepared is considered the author for purposes of this title, and, unless the parties have expressly agreed otherwise in a written instrument signed by them, owns all of the rights comprised in the copyright.

Warner Brothers required Spike Lee to sign a "work for hire" agreement, so that even Lee would not be a co-author and co-owner with Warner Brothers. It would be illogical to conclude that Warner Brothers, while not wanting to permit Lee to own the copyright, intended to share ownership with individuals like Aalmuhammed who worked under Lee's control, especially ones who at the time had made known no claim to the role of co-author.

expectedJSON.body: For a joint work prepared by two or more authors who did not work for hire, the copyright endures for a term consisting of the life of the last surviving author and 70 years after that author's death. This differs from the single-author term (the author's life plus 70 years) and from the fixed term for works made for hire, and it means that a finding of joint authorship can lengthen the copyright term of a work by keying its expiration to the longest-lived co-author.

citations.cite: U.S. Code, Copyright Act, duration of copyright -- joint works
citations.quote: In the case of a joint work prepared by two or more authors who did not work for hire, the copyright endures for a term consisting of the life of the last surviving author and 70 years after such last surviving author's death.

expectedJSON.body: This Information Sheet is a companion to, and does not repeat, several existing documents in this project. The Work Made for Hire Agreement (Independent Contractor), Copyright Assignment Agreement, and Invention Assignment & Confidentiality Agreement documents address how copyright ownership is allocated by written agreement, which -- as the Ninth Circuit observed in Aalmuhammed v. Lee -- is the best objective manifestation of whether collaborators intend to be or not to be co-authors. The Copyright Registration Information Sheet addresses registration of a work, including the joint-work term of copyright, and the Copyright Termination Right Information Sheet addresses the statutory termination of transfers. The Employee Invention Assignment -- Statutory Limits and Shop Right Information Sheet addresses California's limits on assignment of employee inventions, which concern patentable inventions rather than copyright co-ownership. This Information Sheet is limited to the default federal rules on who is a joint author and what co-owners of a copyright may do absent an agreement; it does not address community-property treatment of copyrights between spouses, co-ownership of patents or trademarks, or the moral-rights provisions applicable to joint works of visual art.

Prepared by Jordan T. Reyes concerning the work described above.

This Information Sheet is a general informational reference about the federal rules on joint authorship and co-ownership of copyright. It is not a collaboration agreement, a copyright assignment, a license, or a registration filing, and it is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney about whether a particular work is a joint work, who its authors and co-owners are, or what any co-owner may do in a specific situation.
